generatedProse.concept-context: In practice, learning by doing takes several forms across different subjects. Placements put you into a real workplace or setting. Fieldwork takes you out to gather evidence or observe something first hand. Practical and laboratory work lets you run real procedures, and live projects, such as producing something for a real client, give you real work with real consequences. Each is a different shape of the same idea: you learn a subject by practising it.
generatedProse.worked-example:
Two students are each offered a piece of learning by doing.

Student A is told the activity is 'just a practical exercise' and assumes it does not really count, because it is not a proper placement. Student A almost dismisses it, thinking practice- and work-based learning only ever means one thing.

Student B recognises a live project for a real client as the same kind of learning, in a different form. It is not a placement, but it is real work with real consequences, so it is learning by doing, shaped to fit the subject.

Both were offered practice- and work-based learning. Only Student B saw that it comes in many forms, and that a practical exercise and a live project both count.
generatedProse.summary: Practice- and work-based learning takes many forms: placements, fieldwork, practical and laboratory work, and live projects for real clients. You can now recognise that range and give an example in your own subject. What they share is learning by doing. The next lesson turns to why this kind of learning is so valuable to you.

check.body: In the worked example, what did Student B understand that Student A did not?

items.text: That a live project is learning by doing, just in a different form from a placement.
That a placement is the only real form of learning by doing.
That practice- and work-based learning only counts in one kind of setting.
That the project did not really count as learning.

feedback.correct: That's right. A live project is practice- and work-based learning in a different form from a placement.
feedback.incorrectNotFinal: Not quite. Look for what Student B recognised about the different forms this learning can take.
feedback.incorrectFinal: Student B understood that a live project is practice- and work-based learning in a different form from a placement.

_prompts.concept-context: What does this look like in practice within the given context? Write a short follow-on from the generic definition above, in the learner's own subject or discipline. Keep it to two or three sentences, mid-register, following straight on from the generic definition.
_prompts.worked-example: Give a subject-specific worked example of this lesson's concept: a weaker or less-developed version first, then a stronger version reached by better practice, using the context cast (character tokens) consistently. Keep the weaker-then-stronger shape and the two-part contrast; carry the cast only through the {{learner-a}} (weaker) and {{learner-b}} (stronger) tokens, never a literal name (the pack supplies the whole body, but not the names). Each example paragraph must begin with its token, weaker first - merge-context.js's wrapProse() only emits the we-weaker/we-stronger cue classes for a paragraph that leads with the token. The merge renders it as a block quote, so write it as continuous prose, not as a quoted comment plus commentary.
_prompts.summary: Recap what the learner can now do, in terms of their own subject or context. One short paragraph. Do not restate the learning outcomes verbatim.
_prompts.check: Write the subject's own version of this lesson's check question(s), testing the same outcome in the learner's own discipline. Keep the same number of items and the same correctness pattern as the generic version; reword the stem and items for the subject. Keep the component-level feedback (correct / notFinal / final) teaching, never a bare verdict.
